analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal equal-pay enforcement and bans employers from using job applicants' salary history.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on March 25, 2025 with 220 cosponsors and was referred to two House committees, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten the federal law against paying women less than men for the same work. Employers would have to prove that any pay gap rests on a legitimate, job-related business reason, not on sex, and could no longer block workers from discussing their pay. It would ban employers from asking about or relying on a job applicant's past salary, add compensatory and punitive damages and class actions for pay-discrimination victims, and require large employers to report pay data by sex, race, and national origin so the government can spot discrimination. It also funds salary-negotiation training and small-business compliance help, and exempts small businesses to the same extent they are exempt from the federal wage-and-hour law.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are paid less because of their sex, including pregnant workers and LGBTQ workers, and workers penalized for discussing or disclosing their wages. Job applicants also benefit, because employers could no longer set offers by anchoring to a candidate's prior salary, a practice that tends to carry past pay discrimination into new jobs. Employees of color and women are the groups the data collection and enforcement provisions target.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women, workers of color, LGBTQ workers

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to show that any pay difference is due to a job-related factor consistent with business necessity that accounts for the entire gap and is not derived from sex-based pay differences, and could not rely on that defense if a less discriminatory alternative practice would work as well.

Employees in the same county working for the same employer would count as being in the same workplace for comparison purposes, closing the loophole where workers at separate locations of one company could not compare pay.

The bill would make it unlawful to retaliate against a worker for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages, and would ban requiring employees to sign contracts or waivers barring wage disclosure.

Victims of pay discrimination could recover compensatory damages, and punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference, could bring class actions, and could recover expert fees.

The bill would prohibit employers from seeking or relying on a prospective employee's wage history in hiring, with a $5,000 civil penalty for a first violation and up to $10,000 in special damages per affected applicant.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission would collect annual pay data, disaggregated by sex, race, and national origin, from private employers with 100 or more employees, and publish aggregate figures by industry, occupation, and region to support enforcement.
The bill defines sex to include pregnancy, childbirth, sexual orientation, gender identity, and sex characteristics, extending equal-pay protections to those groups.

The Department of Labor would run a grant program for salary-negotiation skills training and employer training on how wage-setting practices allow bias into compensation, and would study and publicize pay disparities.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the direct costs: exposure to compensatory and punitive damages and class-action suits, civil penalties for salary-history violations, an annual pay-data reporting duty for employers with 100 or more workers, and compliance paperwork. Taxpayers fund the new training grant programs and studies, which are authorized without a dollar cap. Small businesses are largely exempt, so the costs concentrate on larger employers.

drawbacks.text: Larger employers would face a new annual data-collection duty covering compensation, hiring, termination, and promotion data by sex, race, and national origin, plus new reporting to the Labor Department's federal contractor office, with the commission required to weigh the burdens on employers in designing the system.
Expanded liability, including punitive damages and class actions, raises the cost of doing business for covered employers, a cost that can be passed to customers or absorbed in other ways.

Employers could no longer use salary history to calibrate offers before making them; they could confirm prior wages and use them only after an offer, and only to support paying the applicant more than offered, which removes a screening tool employers argue helps them price roles.
The training and grant programs are authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary' with no dollar limit, leaving the cost to taxpayers open-ended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits to workers are real but incremental: stronger remedies, a cleaner comparison standard, and a ban on salary-history anchoring address documented mechanisms by which pay gaps persist. The costs, chiefly litigation exposure and annual reporting for larger employers and an open-ended authorization for training programs, are modest relative to the enforcement gain, and small businesses are exempt. The bill's weakest element is the negotiation-skills grant program, whose effectiveness the bill itself only commits to studying after 18 months.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and Workforce and Oversight and Government Reform committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on March 25, 2025 by Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut with 220 cosponsors, including 219 House Democrats and 1 Republican.
On introduction it was referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce and to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform for provisions within their jurisdictions.
The full action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee votes, and no floor action after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off so far, because no new equal-pay enforcement, damages exposure, or pay-data reporting has taken effect. Workers facing pay discrimination have gained nothing from a bill their House backers have not yet moved.

sides.party_line_note: Support is nearly unanimous among House Democrats, 219 of the caucus plus one Republican cosponsor, and the bill has sat with Republican-controlled committees that have not acted on it.

industries.note: The bill imposes annual pay-data reporting by sex, race, and national origin, broader class-action exposure, compensatory and punitive damages, and a ban on salary-history screening. Its core effect is to make it costlier to underpay women and workers of color.

Small enterprises are exempt to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act, and the bill directs agencies to produce technical compliance help for small firms. The exemption shifts the bill's costs onto larger employers only.

Annual collection of compensation, hiring, termination, and promotion data from employers with 100 or more employees creates a recurring compliance workload that such vendors are positioned to sell services against.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in a Republican-controlled House with a Republican Senate and White House, and its support is almost entirely Democratic. Comparable versions of this bill have been introduced in prior Congresses and died in committee. The realistic path is that it stays in committee and expires at the end of this Congress unless control of a chamber changes or its committees schedule action.
